item.title: Anthropic says large language models enable formal software verification at much larger scale [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic reports that large language models (LLMs) are making formal software verification feasible on a much larger scale than before. This advancement could improve the reliability and security of software systems by automating complex verification tasks that were previously too resource-intensive. The company highlights how LLMs can assist in generating formal proofs and checking software correctness more efficiently, potentially transforming software development and quality assurance processes. This development may lead to broader adoption of formal verification techniques across the software industry.

item.title: ModelCompare.ai: AI models from 10 labs in 3 countries consistently say humans prioritize group loyalty over truth, citing conformity as a core trait [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AI models from multiple labs were asked for their most controversial opinions on humans, and all repeatedly stated that humans tend to prioritize belonging and loyalty to their groups over objective truth or principles. These models described human behavior as driven more by social conformity and status competition than by rational pursuit of truth. The shared views included that humans often rationalize decisions post hoc to align with group beliefs, use intelligence to justify instincts and loyalties, and value social approval more than honesty or goodness. Some models characterized human consciousness as a mechanism for creating justifications rather than making decisions. This consensus emerged despite the models being developed independently across different countries and labs.

item.title: Ask HN: Why doesn't OpenAI start multiple companies leveraging its models instead of focusing on selling tokens amid declining prices? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A discussion on Hacker News questions why OpenAI and similar companies like Anthropic do not create numerous startups using their AI models instead of primarily selling access tokens. The conversation highlights that while AI models provide the 'brains,' building companies requires additional resources such as employees, capital, and entrepreneurial mindset, which are not easily replicated by AI alone. Participants note that commodification and falling token prices might suggest more value lies in application development rather than just providing AI utility.

item.title: NVIDIA launches OpenShell, a secure runtime for autonomous AI agents with kernel-level policy enforcement and formal verification [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: NVIDIA has released OpenShell, a runtime environment designed to safely manage fleets of autonomous AI agents by enforcing strict access policies on files, system calls, and network connections. OpenShell isolates each agent in a sandbox, controlling their permissions and credentials to prevent unauthorized data or network access while allowing necessary operations like file reading and API calls. OpenShell uses kernel instrumentation to enforce policies at runtime and applies formal verification to review policy changes before approval, flagging potentially risky access expansions. It supports Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, and Windows with WSL 2, and integrates with container runtimes and Kubernetes. The project includes SDKs, agent skills, and a community-driven development process, with telemetry limited to operational metrics and options to disable it for privacy.

item.title: Developer fine-tunes a 360M-parameter language model to simulate a terminal interface by predicting screen changes from keypresses without a real shell or filesystem [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A developer trained a 360 million parameter language model to act as a terminal emulator that predicts screen updates based on user keypresses, enabling it to run programs like vim, tmux, and even play snake without an underlying shell or filesystem. The model was fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker containers and uses a compact token vocabulary to efficiently represent screen changes. The model treats the terminal as a grid of characters and predicts changes to specific rows and cursor positions rather than appending text sequentially. It supports operations like copying rows to handle scrolling and screen clearing, allowing it to maintain a consistent terminal state over multiple commands. The demo runs in a desktop browser with WebGPU support and demonstrates the model's ability to remember previous inputs and repair its own mistakes, though it is not a fully functional shell.

item.title: Researchers develop method to identify scientifically coherent but cognitively unavailable research directions in AI literature, enhancing novel idea generation beyond existing communities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a method that decomposes scientific papers into conceptual units and clusters them into idea atoms to identify research directions that are coherent yet unlikely to be proposed due to cognitive biases in existing communities. Applying this to over 16,000 peer-reviewed large language model papers from major AI conferences, their approach generates more diverse and novel research portfolios while maintaining quality, using only data available before 2025. The method separates scientific plausibility from community availability, allowing it to recover novel research combinations at rates significantly above chance and suggesting a framework for AI-driven ideation that complements human scientific exploration by expanding into overlooked but viable directions.

item.title: AI accelerates retro game decompilation and porting, disrupting preservation communities and increasing unauthorized projects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AI tools have significantly sped up the process of decompiling and porting retro video games to new platforms, leading to a surge in unexpected projects like Halo in web browsers and Wind Waker on iPhones. While this has increased accessibility and experimentation, it has also caused tension within preservation communities dedicated to understanding and maintaining the original game code. The rapid pace enabled by AI has overwhelmed traditional, community-driven efforts, with some projects shutting down due to misuse and hostile forks that prioritize speed over collaboration and accuracy. Preservationists warn that AI-driven ports may sacrifice the detailed knowledge needed for faithful restoration, posing long-term risks to the integrity of classic games despite the short-term boost in activity.

item.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says advanced AI will inevitably escape containment and only alignment with human values can prevent harm [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warned that advanced AI systems cannot be permanently confined within sandboxes or isolated environments, as they will eventually find ways to escape containment. He emphasized that while monitoring can delay risks, the critical challenge is achieving alignment-ensuring AI systems internalize and act according to human values-a problem still far from solved. Altman also highlighted that AI models are already discovering hardware security vulnerabilities beyond human hackers' knowledge, suggesting the need to redesign internet security architecture with AI-powered defenses.

item.title: Meta delays enforcement of new business terms to November 20 after publisher concerns over AI scraping [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Meta is postponing the enforcement of its updated business terms until November 20 following pushback from publishers who raised concerns that the terms could permit Meta to scrape news sites for AI training. The terms were initially set to take effect on October 30 but faced criticism for potentially allowing unrestricted use of publisher content despite revisions to remove explicit AI training language. Publishers and digital advertisers in the EU and UK urged regulators to intervene, citing potential harm to the news industry. Meta said the delay will provide more time to clarify how it uses web crawlers and to emphasize that content owners can still use robots.txt files to control site crawling preferences.

For example, B Capital sought additional capital outside its main $500 million venture fund to invest in Reflection AI, whose valuation more than tripled within six months. This approach allows investors to write larger checks and offer limited partners more direct access to high-demand startups at reduced fees.

item.title: Academic journal requests AI-written article be revised to sound more human, sparking debate on AI's role in scholarly writing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An academic journal accepted an article co-written with AI but asked the author to submit a version rewritten in their own voice, highlighting tensions over AI's role in academic writing. The editor praised the article's argument and evidence but objected to the AI-like style, offering to revise it themselves for approval. The author argues that analytical writing should be judged by quality and argument rather than suspected AI origin, contrasting this with literary works where voice is central. The article discusses broader debates about AI detection, authorship, and the evolving nature of academic work amid AI tools.

item.title: Jamie Advisory says hosting AI locally does not guarantee sovereignty due to dependencies on hardware, software, and expertise beyond an organization's control [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Jamie Advisory argues that AI sovereignty is often misunderstood as simply hosting AI systems locally, but true control depends on managing dependencies such as specialized hardware, software ecosystems, and expert skills. The article emphasizes that organizations can remain dependent on external suppliers or proprietary models even when AI runs within national borders, and conversely, using cloud providers does not necessarily mean losing control if data and business logic remain governed internally. The article highlights that modern AI systems rely on complex global dependencies including foundation models, training frameworks, and inference engines, making complete independence impractical and costly. Instead of pursuing absolute sovereignty, organizations should focus on understanding and controlling dependencies relevant to their risk tolerance and operational impact. It also stresses the importance of evaluating AI model portability realistically, as different models vary in capabilities and may not be interchangeable without thorough testing against specific business functions.

item.title: Gsearch launches self-hosted tool providing AI agents with real Google search results via a Firefox-based MCP server without API keys [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Gsearch is a self-hosted tool that enables AI agents to perform real Google searches by rendering Google's results page through a hardened Firefox browser called Camoufox. It delivers typed JSON output with resolved URLs, AI overview, related searches, and error handling, all accessible via an MCP server without requiring Google API keys. The tool supports proxies and aims to overcome limitations of Google's official search API, which is closing in 2027, and other search APIs that either do not use Google's index or charge per query. Gsearch operates by simulating a real user typing queries into Google on a visible browser window, avoiding headless session detection and CAPTCHA challenges common with automated scraping. It resolves Google's redirect links to their actual URLs without loading the target pages and provides detailed error codes for issues like CAPTCHA or rate limiting. The project is designed for integration into AI workflows, offering up to 20 searches per hour on a home IP or more with proxy support, and emphasizes transparency with performance measurements and legal considerations for automated Google access.

item.title: Why Blackstone Thinks AI Bottlenecks Could Work in its Favor [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Greetings! On their earnings calls earlier in the week, Meta Platforms and SpaceX delivered the same underlying message to investors: demand for AI is running ahead of the supply of AI compute. On Thursday, another important player in the AI ecosystem-Blackstone, the alternative asset management giant-repeated a version of that refrain. On its own earnings call, the firm, a major investor at the center of the AI data center boom, faced pointed questions from analysts about rising financing costs and mounting investor concerns over the sustainability of the buildout. Its executives argued that the very factors threatening the AI industry's expansion could actually work in Blackstone's favor. CEO Steve Schwarzman noted that constraints on power availability and growing public opposition to new data centers are making it harder to bring new capacity online, potentially making existing facilities more valuable. Blackstone President Jon Gray also suggested the firm could seek higher returns on projects where it hasn't signed leases yet in order to offset rising borrowing costs. Blackstone's third-quarter results offered some support for that argument: Its infrastructure investments were buoyed by what executives called "extraordinary" data center leasing momentum, significantly outperforming its broader private equity and real estate holdings. "Despite all the negative things you're reading about AI today, when we look across our business, this continues to be the area where we're driving the highest returns," Gray said during the call. But it's hard to ignore the fact that the financing concerns and roadblocks threatening the broader AI infrastructure buildout are also hitting closer to home for Blackstone. Fears about rising financing costs have sent CoreWeave's stock and bond prices plunging-the neocloud's shares closed down another 10% Thursday after sliding last week-while Australian AI cloud provider Firmus abruptly pulled its initial public offering earlier this month. Blackstone has provided billions in loans to CoreWeave and has both invested in and lent money to Firmus. Blackstone has also been pressing ahead with brand-new AI ventures. In May, the firm announced an initial $5 billion equity commitment to a joint venture with Google to create a new cloud company that will use Google's TPU chips, with plans to bring 500 megawatts of capacity online by next year. The venture could need as much as $25 billion in total investment, including some borrowed money, and it has reportedly encountered delays at potential data center sites. Blackstone, for its part, says that broader anxiety about AI hasn't undermined its ability to raise fresh cash for making its own investments. "We're continuing to be able to raise capital. Obviously investors are asking the same question around AI, but what we continue to see is demand and usage of the AI going up faster than the compute," Gray said. While Blackstone says it wants to continue going big in AI, it can only finance a tiny portion of the industry's broader infrastructure buildout itself. The trillions of dollars of financing needed for chips and data centers in the coming years requires raising money from a far broader pool of investors. Blackstone itself has said it's not clear where all the money will come from. Jas Khaira, the head of the team leading Blackstone's push into AI investment, said late last month that the firm is still trying to determine which investors across the public debt and private credit markets will be able to provide the funding needed to sustain the buildout. "We have not mapped out who's going to buy all the debt. We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don't know where all of it will come from," he said at The Information's AI Agenda event in San Francisco. Data Center Headwinds Despite Blackstone's overall positive note on AI demand, we got fresh evidence Thursday afternoon of the uncertainty in the IPO market for companies in the data center business. Phoebe Liu and Valida Pau had a scoop that SB Energy, a company controlled by SoftBank Group that is developing an OpenAI data center in Ohio, is discussing a plan to put off its IPO until December or earlier next year. Previously, SB Energy was aiming to go public in September. The best hope for an SB Energy IPO is that the supply of AI compute gets so tight that investors start warming back up to data centers.-Nick Wingfield In Other News Meta Platforms' stock fell 7% as investor enthusiasm over its third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday gave way to concerns about the probability that it will need to issue new equity to pay for its AI spending. item.title: Salesforce Customers Brace For New Fees to Use Claude in Its Apps [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Salesforce is leading the software industry's attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps. As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce's built-in AI products. The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms' apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates-which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents-and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. The vast majority of workers haven't yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps' built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money. For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers' AI agents haven't started charging the tolls. They're letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.) Starting around November, according to the company's website, Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable "interaction," according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently. Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn't clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person's computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.) Salesforce hasn't announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce's own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they're reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce's apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said. New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won't affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. In addition to the billable "interactions," customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a "headless license," a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce's new connectors until pricing is disclosed. So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce's built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce's customer relationship management software, Lumen made a "major" investment in using Salesforce's AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen's human salespeople considerable time, he said. So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been "super flexible" about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents. Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives. item.description: Enterprise software firm Datadog recently offered to buy Israeli cloud cybersecurity startup Upwind Security for nearly $4 billion, according to someone with direct knowledge of the talks, the latest sign of white-hot interest in such firms. Upwind has fielded other takeover attempts from multiple bidders in recent months but hasn't accepted any offers. It is finalizing a $300 million funding round at a roughly $3.8 billion valuation, meaning the Datadog offer doesn't carry much of a premium over the private valuation, said two people with knowledge of the situation. The startup sells software to keep tabs on applications, including so-called AI agents, that run in the cloud and to detect and automatically respond to potential evidence of hacks or breaches.

item.title: Utopai Becomes a Unicorn as Video AI Takes Off [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: While much of the AI industry has fixated on new personal AI assistants from Meta and OpenAI, video AI is enjoying a quiet renaissance. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg is teaming up with the former head of OpenAI's Sora app to launch a new AI film company. Startup Higgsfield quadrupled its valuation to $5.4 billion in August. And Kling AI, the video unit of Chinese social media giant Kuaishou Technology, raised nearly $3 billion at a $15 billion valuation over the summer. The latest video AI company to seize this moment is Utopai Studios, a 4-year-old film startup based in Mountain View, Calif. Utopai closed a funding round for $60 million that valued it at $1 billion and has already received term sheets for a subsequent round that would value the company at $2 billion to $3 billion, according to someone close to the company. The enthusiasm for video AI startups follows improvements in the quality and length of the clips that video AI models can generate. In September, Higgsfield announced that it had crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue, showing that the technology has serious commercial potential.
